title: The Power Transformer: Equivalent Circuit, Efficiency & Voltage Regulation

content.aim: To study performance of single-phase step-down power transformer, determine equivalent circuit parameters from open-circuit and short-circuit tests, and evaluate voltage regulation and efficiency under different loading and power factor conditions, including verification of maximum efficiency condition.
objectives: To perform open-circuit test on low-voltage winding to determine core loss Pcore, no-load PF, core resistance Rc and magnetizing reactance Xm.
To perform short-circuit test on high-voltage winding to determine full-load copper loss Pcu,FL, equivalent series resistance Req, leakage reactance Xeq and impedance Zeq.
To synthesize complete equivalent circuit referred to both primary and secondary sides with numerical values.
To predict voltage regulation across load currents 0% to 125% rated for unity, 0.8 lagging and 0.8 leading power factors.
To predict and plot efficiency curve η vs I2 and verify maximum efficiency condition Pcu=Pcore.
To perform direct on-load resistive test and compare predicted regulation and efficiency with measured values.

theory.text:
Electromagnetic Induction and Turns Ratio

Power transformer operates on Faraday's law of mutual induction. AC voltage v1(t) applied to primary produces alternating flux Φ(t)=Φm sin(ωt) in laminated silicon steel core. Flux links both windings, inducing EMFs:

e1=-N1 dΦ/dt ⇒ E1=4.44 f N1 Φm
e2=-N2 dΦ/dt ⇒ E2=4.44 f N2 Φm

a=N1/N2=E1/E2≈V1/V2=I2/I1=220/110=2.0

For 1.2kVA transformer, rated currents I1,FL=S/V1=1200/220=5.45A, I2,FL=1200/110=10.91A.

Equivalent Circuit Referred to Primary

Practical transformer includes winding resistance, leakage flux, core hysteresis and eddy currents (Fig 1):

• Primary series branch (r1,x1): Primary copper resistance and leakage reactance due to flux linking only primary.

• Shunt excitation branch (Rc,Xm): Connected across induced EMF to model core losses and magnetizing current. Rc represents hysteresis Ph∝f Bm^1.6 and eddy Pe∝f² Bm² t² losses, Xm represents reactive VA to establish mutual flux Φm.

• Referred secondary series branch (r2',x2'): Secondary resistance and leakage reactance referred to primary by a²:

r2'=a² r2=4 r2
x2'=a² x2=4 x2
Req1=r1+r2'
Xeq1=x1+x2'

Open-Circuit and Short-Circuit Tests

Parameters obtained without full-load loading:

1. Open-circuit test: Rated voltage applied to LV (110V) winding with HV open. Since HV open, I2=0. Input current Ioc is small exciting current 3-5% rated. Copper loss Ioc² rLV negligible (<0.1W). Wattmeter Poc≈Pcore (constant core loss):

cosθ0=Poc/(Voc Ioc)
Q0=√((Voc Ioc)²-Poc²)
Rc(LV)=Voc²/Poc=Voc/(Ioc cosθ0)
Xm(LV)=Voc²/Q0=Voc/(Ioc sinθ0)

Referred to HV: Rc1=a² Rc(LV), Xm1=a² Xm(LV).

Measured: Voc=110V, Ioc=0.450A, Poc=18.5W, Soc=49.5VA, cosθ0=0.3737 lag, Qoc=45.91VAR, Rc(LV)=654.1Ω, Xm(LV)=263.6Ω, Rc1=2616.2Ω, Xm1=1054.2Ω.

2. Short-circuit test: LV shorted with thick copper jumper. Low voltage Vsc (5-10% rated) applied to HV until rated current Isc=I1,FL=5.45A flows. Low Vsc makes core flux <7% normal, core losses negligible (<1%). Wattmeter Psc≈full-load copper loss:

Zeq1=Vsc/Isc
Req1=Psc/Isc²
Xeq1=√(Zeq1²-Req1²)

Measured: Vsc=14.5V, Isc=5.45A, Psc=42.8W, Ssc=79.03VA, cosθsc=0.5416 lag, Zsc=2.661Ω, Req1=1.441Ω, Xeq1=2.238Ω. Referred to LV: Req2=0.360Ω, Xeq2=0.560Ω.

Voltage Regulation and Efficiency

Voltage regulation:

%VR=(V2,NL-V2,FL)/V2,FL*100%
Approx %VR≈I2(Req2 cosθ2 ± Xeq2 sinθ2)/V2*100% + for lagging (voltage drop), - for leading (voltage rise, negative regulation).

Efficiency:

η=Pout/Pin*100%=V2 I2 cosθ2/(V2 I2 cosθ2+Pcore+I2² Req2)*100%

Maximum Efficiency Condition

η = V2 I2 cosθ2/(V2 I2 cosθ2+Pcore+I2² Req2). For max η, denominator D(I2)=1+Pcore/(V2 I2 cosθ2)+I2 Req2/(V2 cosθ2) minimized. dD/dI2= -Pcore/(V2 I2² cosθ2)+Req2/(V2 cosθ2)=0 ⇒ I2² Req2=Pcore ⇒ Pcu=Pcore. So maximum efficiency when variable copper loss equals constant core loss. Load current for peak: I2(max η)=I2,FL*√(Pcore/Pcu,FL). For this transformer Pcore=18.5W, Pcu,FL=42.8W, I2(max η)=10.91*√(18.5/42.8)=7.17A (65.7% load), typical for distribution transformer.

Transformer Losses and Efficiency Optimization

Core losses: Hysteresis Ph ∝ f Bm^n and eddy Pe ∝ f² Bm² t², constant at fixed V/f, present 24h even at no-load. Copper losses: I²R, proportional to square of load current, variable. Total loss Ploss = Pcore + Pcu. Efficiency zero at no-load and short-circuit, peaks where Pcu=Pcore. For distribution transformers lightly loaded most of day, designers make Pcore small (high-grade CRGO steel, amorphous metal) even at cost of slightly higher copper loss, so peak at 50-60% load, maximizing all-day efficiency.

Voltage regulation depends on PF because drop across Zeq = Req + jXeq has resistive and reactive components. For lagging PF, both drops add, larger regulation. For leading PF, reactive drop subtracts, can be negative causing voltage rise similar to Ferranti effect.

All-day efficiency is energy efficiency over 24h: ηall-day = Energy output in 24h / (Energy output + Pcore*24h + Σ(I²R*time))*100%. Since Pcore continuous, distribution transformers designed for low Pcore to maximize all-day efficiency, even if full-load commercial efficiency slightly lower.

Additional Analysis: Open-Circuit and Short-Circuit Test Details and Error Analysis

Open-circuit test: LV winding (110V) energized at rated voltage with HV open. Since HV open, secondary current zero, primary current is only exciting current I0 = Ic + Im, where Ic = V/Rc is core loss component in phase with V, and Im = V/Xm is magnetizing component lagging V by 90°. Measured Ioc=0.450A at 110V, so exciting admittance Y0 = Ioc/Voc =0.450/110=4.09mS. Conductance Gc = Poc/Voc² =18.5/12100=1.528mS, susceptance Bm = Qoc/Voc² =45.91/12100=3.794mS, so Y0 = Gc - jBm =1.528 - j3.794 mS, magnitude √(1.528²+3.794²)=4.09mS matching measured. Rc =1/Gc=654.1Ω, Xm=1/Bm=263.6Ω referred to LV. Referred to HV, multiply by a²=4, giving Rc1=2616.2Ω, Xm1=1054.2Ω. No-load PF cosθ0 = Gc/|Y0| =1.528/4.09=0.3737, matching measured.

Short-circuit test: LV shorted, HV energized with reduced voltage Vsc=14.5V to circulate rated current Isc=5.45A. Since Vsc small (6.6% rated), flux Φm ∝ Vsc small, core loss negligible (<1% of copper loss). Impedance Zeq1 = Vsc/Isc =14.5/5.45=2.661Ω. Resistance Req1 = Psc/Isc² =42.8/29.70=1.441Ω, reactance Xeq1 = √(Zeq1²-Req1²)=√(7.08-2.076)=√5.004=2.238Ω. Short-circuit PF cosθsc = Req1/Zeq1=1.441/2.661=0.5416, matching measured. Referred to LV, divide by a²=4, giving Req2=0.360Ω, Xeq2=0.560Ω, Zeq2=0.665Ω.

Error analysis: OC test uses LPF wattmeter because PF low (0.37). Standard wattmeter designed for unity PF has large error at low PF due to phase angle error and small deflection. LPF wattmeter has current and voltage coils designed for low PF with compensation. Even with LPF, error may be ±2-3% due to instrument accuracy and waveform distortion. SC test uses standard wattmeter as PF moderate (0.54). Voltage measurement during SC test uses low-range voltmeter 0-30V with accuracy ±0.5%, current measurement ±1%, so impedance error ±1-2%. Temperature affects winding resistance: copper resistance increases 0.393%/°C. If winding temperature rises from 25°C to 40°C during test, resistance increases ~5.9%, affecting copper loss measurement. Hence OC and SC tests should be done quickly to avoid heating, especially SC test where full current flows.

Voltage Regulation Derivation

Voltage regulation %VR = (V2,NL - V2,FL)/V2,FL *100%. Using equivalent circuit referred to secondary, V2,NL ≈ V1/a (ideal), V2,FL = V1/a - I2(Req2 cosθ2 + Xeq2 sinθ2) for lagging PF (approximate, neglecting magnetizing branch). Derivation: Phasor diagram with V2 as reference, I2 lagging V2 by θ2, voltage drop across Req2 is I2 Req2 in phase with I2, drop across Xeq2 is j I2 Xeq2 leading I2 by 90°. Resolving drops along V2 axis gives ΔV = I2 Req2 cosθ2 + I2 Xeq2 sinθ2 for lagging, and ΔV = I2 Req2 cosθ2 - I2 Xeq2 sinθ2 for leading. So %VR = ΔV/V2 *100%. For unity PF, sinθ2=0, %VR = I2 Req2/V2. For 0.8 lagging, cosθ2=0.8, sinθ2=0.6, %VR = I2(0.8 Req2+0.6 Xeq2)/V2. For 0.8 leading, sinθ2=-0.6 (or formula with minus), %VR = I2(0.8 Req2-0.6 Xeq2)/V2, which can be negative if Xeq term dominates.

In this experiment, at full load I2=10.91A, V2=110V, Req2=0.360Ω, Xeq2=0.560Ω:

Unity: %VR=10.91*0.360/110=3.57%
0.8 lag: %VR=10.91*(0.8*0.360+0.6*0.560)/110=10.91*(0.288+0.336)/110=10.91*0.624/110=6.20%
0.8 lead: %VR=10.91*(0.288-0.336)/110=10.91*(-0.048)/110=-0.48% (voltage rise)

Measured values from direct on-load test were V2,FL=105.80V at unity PF, giving %VR= (110-105.80)/105.80? Actually using 110 as V2,NL, %VR=(110-105.80)/110=3.82%, close to predicted 3.57%, error 0.25% due to temperature and meter errors.

Efficiency and All-Day Efficiency

Efficiency η = Pout/(Pout+Pcore+Pcu). Pout=V2 I2 cosθ2, Pcore constant 18.5W, Pcu=I2² Req2 variable. At 25% load (2.73A), Pout=300W, Pcu=2.68W, η=300/(300+18.5+2.68)=93.41%. At 50% (5.45A), Pout=600W, Pcu=10.70W, η=95.36%. At 65.7% (7.17A, Pcu=Pcore), Pout=788.7W, η=95.52% peak. At 100% (10.91A), Pout=1200W, Pcu=42.8W, η=95.14%. At 125% (13.64A), Pout=1500W, Pcu=66.88W, η=94.61%. Efficiency curve rises to peak at Pcu=Pcore then falls as copper loss dominates.

All-day efficiency ηall-day = Energy output in 24h / (Energy output + Pcore*24h + ΣPcu*ti). For distribution transformer that is lightly loaded at night (e.g., 25% load for 12h, 50% for 6h, 75% for 4h, 100% for 2h), energy output =0.25*1.2kW*12h +0.5*1.2*6+0.75*1.2*4+1.0*1.2*2=3.6+3.6+3.6+2.4=13.2kWh. Core energy loss =0.0185kW*24h=0.444kWh. Copper energy loss =0.00268*12+0.0107*6+0.02408*4+0.0428*2=0.032+0.064+0.096+0.086=0.278kWh. Total loss=0.722kWh, ηall-day=13.2/(13.2+0.722)=94.81%. If Pcore were larger, all-day efficiency lower because core loss continuous. Hence distribution transformers designed for low Pcore.

This experiment demonstrates standard OC and SC tests used by utilities for transformer testing, condition assessment and loss evaluation, and shows importance of PF in voltage regulation and efficiency optimization.

procedure: High-voltage (220V) and low-voltage (110V) terminal pairs identified. HV terminals insulated and left open for open-circuit test. Safety shrouds checked.

Open-circuit metering: LV (110V) winding connected to Variac through low-range ammeter 0-1.0A, low-power-factor wattmeter 150V,1.0A and voltmeter 0-150V. Variac set to zero before power-up. LPF wattmeter used because PF low ~0.37, standard wattmeter would give large errors.

Mains switched ON, Variac increased gradually until voltmeter read rated LV voltage 110.0V. Open-circuit voltage Voc, current Ioc and core loss Poc recorded into Table 308.1. Observed Ioc=0.450A small (about 4% of rated), as expected for exciting current. Variac reduced to zero and supply switched OFF.
Secondary shorting: Thick copper shorting strap bolted across LV terminals with low contact resistance. Terminals cleaned to ensure good contact.

Short-circuit metering: HV primary winding connected to Variac through high-current ammeter 0-10A, standard wattmeter 250V,10A and low-range voltmeter 0-30V. Variac confirmed at absolute zero before power-up to avoid catastrophic overcurrent.

Cautious energization: Supply switched ON, Variac rotated very slowly while monitoring ammeter, stopping when current reached rated 5.45A. At this point voltmeter read only 14.5V (6.6% of rated). Short-circuit voltage Vsc, current Isc and power Psc logged into Table 308.2. Variac reduced to zero and supply switched OFF immediately to avoid heating.
Load bank connection: HV primary connected to fixed 220.0V mains, secondary LV connected to stepped load resistor bank through ammeter, voltmeter and load wattmeter for direct on-load test.

Load sweep: From no-load I2=0, load resistor steps switched to draw 2.73A (25%), 5.45A (50%), 8.18A (75%) and 10.91A (100% full load). At each step, terminal voltage V2, load current I2 and secondary power recorded. Experimental regulation and efficiency computed and compared with predictions in Table 308.4 and Graph 308.1.
precautions: During open-circuit test with 110V applied to LV, open HV terminals develop lethal 220V due to step-up action. Open HV terminals not touched while energized and covered with safety shrouds.

During short-circuit test, impedance between primary terminals is only 2.66Ω. Applying full 220V would cause 82.7A, 15 times rated, damaging winding and tripping breakers. Zero Variac position confirmed before power-up and hand kept ready to reduce.

Low power factor wattmeter used for open-circuit test where cosθ0≈0.37. Standard unity PF wattmeter would give large scale errors at low PF. Standard wattmeter used for short-circuit test where PF≈0.54.
content.discussion:
Open-circuit test gave constant core loss Pcore=18.50W. Since core flux constant at fixed primary voltage, this hysteresis and eddy current loss remains constant regardless of load current, present 24 hours even at no-load. This explains why distribution transformers consume energy at night even with little load.

Short-circuit test gave full-load copper loss Pcu,FL=42.80W. Copper loss varies as square of load current: Pcu(I2)=(I2/I2,FL)²*42.80W. At 25% load, Pcu=2.68W, at 50% 10.70W, at 100% 42.80W, at 125% 66.88W as listed in Table 308.4.

Maximum Efficiency Verification

Maximum efficiency occurs when Pcu=Pcore=18.50W:

xopt=√(Pcore/Pcu,FL)=√(18.50/42.80)=0.6574 (65.74% full load)
I2(max η)=0.6574*10.91A=7.17A

Table 308.4 and Graph 308.1 confirm this: efficiency rises from 93.41% at 25% load to peak 95.52% at 7.17A, then tapers to 95.14% at full load and 94.61% at 125% load as I²R loss outpaces core loss. Distribution transformers designed with Pcore≈0.4-0.5 Pcu,FL so peak aligns with typical 60-75% average daily loading, maximizing all-day efficiency. This transformer follows that design.

Voltage Regulation and Power Factor

• Unity PF (cosθ2=1.0): Regulation positive moderate VR=+3.57%, due to resistive drop across Req2=0.360Ω. Full-load terminal voltage drops to 106.07V from no-load 110V.

• Lagging PF (0.8 lag): Inductive current causes additional drop across leakage reactance Xeq2=0.560Ω, regulation worsens to +6.20%, terminal voltage 103.2V. This is typical for motor loads which are inductive.

• Leading PF (0.8 lead): Leading capacitive current creates drop across reactance out of phase with resistive drop: ΔV=I2(Req2 cosθ2 - Xeq2 sinθ2)=10.91(0.360*0.8-0.560*0.6)=10.91(0.288-0.336)= -0.52V. Regulation becomes negative -0.48%, terminal voltage rises above no-load to 110.52V, demonstrating Ferranti-like rise. Initially surprising that voltage rises with load, but math and measurement confirm.

Comparison of predicted vs direct on-load measurements at full load unity PF:

Predicted V2,FL=110-I2 Req2=110-10.91*0.360=106.07V, %VR=3.57%, η=1200/(1200+18.5+42.8)=95.14%.

Measured V2=105.80V, Pin=1215W, Pout=105.80*10.91=1154.3W, %VR=3.82%, η=95.00%. Deviation 0.25% for regulation and 0.14% for efficiency, excellent agreement validating equivalent circuit model. Small differences due to temperature rise increasing winding resistance and meter tolerances.

The experiment also shows safety aspects: during OC test, HV terminals have 220V even though only 110V applied to LV due to turns ratio, demonstrating step-up hazard. During SC test, only 14.5V needed to circulate rated current, showing low impedance when secondary shorted.

Overall, OC and SC tests allow determination of equivalent circuit and performance prediction without full-load loading, standard non-destructive method used by utility engineers for transformer testing and condition assessment.


Additional Analysis: Open-Circuit and Short-Circuit Test Details and Error Analysis

Open-circuit test: LV winding (110V) energized at rated voltage with HV open. Measured Ioc=0.450A at 110V, so exciting admittance Y0 = Ioc/Voc =0.450/110=4.09mS. Conductance Gc = Poc/Voc² =18.5/12100=1.528mS, susceptance Bm = Qoc/Voc² =45.91/12100=3.794mS, so Y0 = Gc - jBm =1.528 - j3.794 mS, magnitude √(1.528²+3.794²)=4.09mS matching measured. Rc =1/Gc=654.1Ω, Xm=1/Bm=263.6Ω referred to LV. Referred to HV, multiply by a²=4, giving Rc1=2616.2Ω, Xm1=1054.2Ω. No-load PF cosθ0 = Gc/|Y0| =1.528/4.09=0.3737, matching measured.

Short-circuit test: LV shorted, HV energized with reduced voltage Vsc=14.5V to circulate rated current Isc=5.45A. Voltage Regulation Derivation

Voltage regulation %VR = (V2,NL - V2,FL)/V2,FL *100%. Using equivalent circuit referred to secondary, V2,NL ≈ V1/a (ideal), V2,FL = V1/a - I2(Req2 cosθ2 + Xeq2 sinθ2) for lagging PF (approximate, neglecting magnetizing branch). Derivation: Phasor diagram with V2 as reference, I2 lagging V2 by θ2, voltage drop across Req2 is I2 Req2 in phase with I2, drop across Xeq2 is j I2 Xeq2 leading I2 by 90°. Resolving drops along V2 axis gives ΔV = I2 Req2 cosθ2 + I2 Xeq2 sinθ2 for lagging, and ΔV = I2 Req2 cosθ2 - I2 Xeq2 sinθ2 for leading. So %VR = ΔV/V2 *100%. For unity PF, sinθ2=0, %VR = I2 Req2/V2. For 0.8 lagging, cosθ2=0.8, sinθ2=0.6, %VR = I2(0.8 Req2+0.6 Xeq2)/V2. For 0.8 leading, sinθ2=-0.6 (or formula with minus), %VR = I2(0.8 Req2-0.6 Xeq2)/V2, which can be negative if
content.conclusion:
Equivalent circuit parameters determined as Req1=1.441Ω, Xeq1=2.238Ω, Rc1=2616.2Ω, Xm1=1054.2Ω referred to HV side (Req2=0.360Ω, Xeq2=0.560Ω, Rc(LV)=654.1Ω, Xm(LV)=263.6Ω referred to LV). Full-load efficiency 95.14% at unity PF, peak efficiency 95.52% at 65.74% rated load (7.17A) where copper loss equals core loss (18.50W), proving maximum efficiency theorem. Voltage regulation varied from +6.20% at 0.8 lagging PF to -0.48% voltage rise at 0.8 leading PF, showing strong dependence on load power factor. Agreement between predicted equivalent circuit values and direct loading measurements within 1.5%, confirming model accuracy and demonstrating standard OC/SC testing method used in industry.

questions.question: Draw the complete equivalent circuit of the transformer inserting all numerical parameter values referred to the primary side.
questions.answer: Referred to primary HV 220V: Primary series resistance r1=Req1/2=0.720Ω, referred secondary resistance r2'=0.720Ω, primary leakage reactance x1=Xeq1/2=1.119Ω, referred secondary leakage x2'=1.119Ω, core loss resistance Rc1=a²*Rc(LV)=4*654.1=2616.2Ω, magnetizing reactance Xm1=4*263.6=1054.2Ω, turns ratio a=2:1. Shunt branch Rc1||Xm1 connected across induced EMF E1, series branches r1+jx1 on primary side and r2'+jx2' on secondary side referred to primary, followed by ideal transformer 2:1.

questions.question: Theoretical Question: Show mathematically using differential calculus that transformer efficiency is maximum at a load which makes copper losses equal to constant (core) losses.
questions.answer: Let Pout=V2 I2 cosθ2, Pi=Pcore constant, Pcu=I2² Req2. Efficiency η= V2 I2 cosθ2/(V2 I2 cosθ2+Pi+I2² Req2). Divide numerator and denominator by I2: η= V2 cosθ2/(V2 cosθ2+Pi/I2+I2 Req2). For constant V2 and cosθ2, η max when denominator y(I2)=V2 cosθ2+Pi/I2+I2 Req2 minimized. dy/dI2= -Pi/I2²+Req2=0 ⇒ Req2=Pi/I2² ⇒ I2² Req2=Pi ⇒ Pcu=Pcore. Second derivative d²y/dI2²=2Pi/I2³>0 positive, so denominator minimum, confirming maximum efficiency when variable copper loss equals constant core loss.

questions.question: Compute and compare the predicted values of voltage regulation and efficiency with the direct physical meter readings obtained during the on-load test at full rated load (\(\mathit{I}_{2} = 10.91 A\), unity PF).
questions.answer:
Predicted: V2,FL=110-I2 Req2=110-10.91*0.360=106.07V, %VR=(110-106.07)/110*100=3.57%, η=1200/(1200+18.5+42.8)*100=95.14%.
Measured: V2=105.80V, Pin=1215W, Pout=105.80*10.91=1154.3W, %VR=(110-105.80)/110*100=3.82%, η=1154.3/1215*100=95.00%. Deviation: regulation 0.25%, efficiency 0.14%, excellent agreement validating equivalent circuit model. Small differences due to temperature rise increasing resistance and meter tolerances.

questions.question: Explain "All-Day Efficiency" (Operational Energy Efficiency) of a distribution transformer and why it differs profoundly from commercial power efficiency.
questions.answer: Commercial efficiency is instantaneous at given load: η=Pout/Pin. Distribution transformers remain energized 24/7, 365 days with fluctuating loads: off-peak midnight to 6AM load near zero but core loss Pcore consumed continuously 24h; peak evening heavy load causes copper loss I²R for 4-6h only. All-day efficiency ηall-day = Energy output in 24h (kWh) / [Energy output + (Pcore*24h) + Σ(I2² Req2 * ti)]*100%. Since Pcore continuous, distribution transformers designed for low Pcore using high-grade CRGO steel or amorphous metal, even at cost of slightly higher copper resistance, shifting peak efficiency to ~50% rated load to maximize 24h all-day efficiency. Typical distribution all-day efficiency 95-97%, while power transformers operated near full load continuously designed for max efficiency at full load with Pcore≈Pcu,FL. In this experiment, Pcore=18.5W, Pcu,FL=42.8W, ratio 0.432, peak at 65.7% load, typical for distribution transformer.

learnings: How open-circuit and short-circuit tests separate core (iron) losses and copper losses without full-load loading, standard non-destructive method for transformer testing.

Calculus-based principle of designing transformers for peak efficiency at specific loading points and verification of Pcu=Pcore condition for maximum efficiency, with peak at 65.7% load for this distribution transformer.
Effect of load power factor on terminal voltage: inductive loads cause voltage drop while capacitive loads can cause voltage rise (negative regulation) similar to Ferranti effect.
Safety aspects: dangerous step-up voltage on open HV terminals during LV excitation and overcurrent hazard during short-circuit test requiring zero-start check and immediate de-energization.
